## TL;DR

Task cards and the task drawer now recover an in-flight handoff from the server’s persisted handoff status. A reloaded page can show the handoff step, elapsed time, and check progress even when no handoff SSE event was received and the check-run history is empty. The drawer suppresses the auto-repair “stuck” interpretation while RepoOS owns the handoff. Existing check output markers are copied into the durable handoff status so reloads can also restore the step and test-file progress. The progress indicator uses native `<progress>` when totals are known and keeps a readable label when they are not.

## Work and rationale

The task report described a concrete gap between two existing server views. `readHandoffStatus` already persists and serves the state used by `repoos handoff-status`, while the UI inferred handoff ownership from live `task.progress` events or a `handoff-finalize` row in check history. The latter row is not guaranteed: `runHandoffFinalization` creates it only when the optional task-check manager and event listener are supplied. Some server handoff callers run the check without both dependencies, so `/checks` can legitimately return an empty run list while the server’s handoff-status record says `running`. I kept the status record as the durable source rather than adding another store or relying on the check history.

The repo store now hydrates `/api/tasks/:id/handoff-status` and uses a running result in `handoffInFlight`. Active cards fetch the status on mount, then poll only after it reports a running handoff; this avoids adding recurring timers to every idle task card. The drawer refreshes the status alongside its existing check polling. Terminal status results clear stale client-side step state, while absent or incomplete responses do not overwrite a live SSE step. This keeps CLI requests and reloads visible without making an empty test response erase a real event.

The finalizer now parses the existing `::repoos-check-progress::` stream markers and snapshots their JSON into the durable status record. The UI can restore the overall step and test-file counts from that snapshot. It also falls back to the active `handoff-finalize` task-check entry where one exists. The drawer status region and card display a progress bar and text; the text includes the step count and test-file count when available. The card and drawer use the same “running checks · step · elapsed” label. Quiet/stuck repair hints are suppressed while handoff status is running. A test verifies a CLI-origin running status and its progress survive a fresh read of the persisted record.

## Approaches tried

I first relied on the live step and hydrated run list, which reproduced the original reload gap. I then used the durable server status directly and retained task-check history as a richer fallback for paths where it is present. A first polling implementation created a timer for every active card; the idle-board budget test correctly rejected that, so polling is now started only when the first status response says the handoff is running. I also initially changed all handoff labels without preserving the richer test-run progress wording. Focused card/drawer tests exposed both the timer regression and label drift; I aligned both surfaces and kept progress counts in the card hint and bar.

## Challenges and blockers

The first scoped check caught these interaction regressions in existing tests, and a subsequent check caught mismatches where old assertions encoded the former generic “checking” text. I used focused tests to isolate the cases, updated the expectations to the requested “running checks · step” language, and reran the full scoped gate. The final required gate passed. No runtime device or account was needed.

## Key learnings

The task check history is useful for output and timing but is not a complete ownership signal: creation depends on optional instrumentation passed by each handoff caller. Durable ownership should come from the handoff status record. UI polling should be conditional on actual server ownership; per-card recurring timers are enough to invalidate idle-board behavior even if each request is small. Finally, an active handoff check and a quiet engineer are not contradictory states: the server owns progress after handoff, so silence must not be treated as a stalled engineering turn.
